source.title: Theory of Hallucinations based on Equivariance

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Figures are referenced, but their plotted data points are not numerically available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to a character-substitution-cipher task and its custom cross-entropy measure of equivariance acquisition, rather than standard language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The measured Test Loss is cross-entropy for dictionary reconstruction in a character-cipher task, which the paper distinguishes from conventional language-model cross-entropy. The paper reports a power-law pattern for this custom measure. It does not test standard held-out pretraining loss, validate predictions on larger runs, or measure a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The study varies T5 size (16M, 30M, 60M) and training-set size (N=1, 8, 16) on a character-cipher dictionary-reconstruction task. It reports that test cross-entropy follows a power law, which bears on V5, whether the power-law form holds outside text pretraining. The evidence is thin: three points per axis, figures only, no fitted exponents and no uncertainty.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The author reports a power law similar to Kaplan et al. for the custom cipher-reconstruction loss. By extreme, unverified extrapolation, the author estimates that more than 2B parameters, or more than 6.3×10^8 training tokens, would bring the loss below 0.1. The work is framed as a toy model.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses T5 on a character-substitution-cipher dictionary-reconstruction task and measures a newly defined cross-entropy loss, rather than measuring ordinary language-model pretraining loss or fixed-compute optima.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is for a custom toy-task measure, not ordinary pretraining loss. Numeric points are not available in the supplied figures/text, no uncertainty estimates or controls are reported, and the author describes the extrapolations as extreme and requiring further verification.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss; the measure is cipher dictionary-reconstruction loss.
Extrapolations to 2B parameters and N≈300 are stated but never checked against larger runs.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.

Only one toy cipher task is tested, with three points per axis. Other modalities, repeated data and transfer are not tested. No exponent is fitted, so the 'same form' cannot be compared quantitatively.
No comparison of fitting choices or setups.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence quality is very low: a single author, laptop-scale runs, three sizes and three dataset sizes, no fitted exponents, no error bars, and 'local minima' of the loss rather than final values. Whether the T5 checkpoints were pretrained before the vocabulary change is unclear. The extrapolations should not be read as a test of V2.

versions.untested_parts: Standard held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No larger runs are conducted to validate predictions of their loss from smaller runs. The paper gives unverified extrapolations for its custom cipher-task measure.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
The study does not vary depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests a character-level cipher-deciphering task only; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study does not compare fitting choices or setups to test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on them.

relationships.reason: The author states a power law is discerned on log-log plots across parameter count (r1–r3) and dataset size (r3–r5). The support is weak: three points per axis, figure-only, with no fit or uncertainty.
relationships.display_finding: Log-log plots suggested power-law relationships with parameter count and dataset size, each based on three points.
